articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: American admiral Samuel J. Paparo, who leads US Indo-Pacific Command, is in India from 3 to 8 October. It is his second visit this year.
The US Embassy said the trip is meant to push forward the "major defense partnership" and deepen cooperation between the two militaries.
Its list of topics includes digital transformation, emerging technologies and regional strategic stability. It also names "defense energy resilience" and an "increasingly competitive technology landscape", though it does not spell out what either would involve.
Press release by the US Embassy in India.
On his earlier trip, Paparo visited Delhi, Chandimandir and Bengaluru. He met the Chief of Defence Staff and the Navy chief, and discussed security along India's western and northern borders.
Last month, Paparo conducted a series of key bilateral and multilateral meetings on the sidelines of the 28th Indo-Pacific Chiefs of defence conference in Victoria, Canada, held from August 31 to September 2.
According to the US Pacific Command (US PACOM), Paparo highlighted "the importance of strong bilateral and multilateral relationships in advancing regional security and deterrence".
Throughout the conference, the US commander engaged in discussions with the Defence Cooperation Council and the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad), and joined military leadership from Asean nations. 
Paparo also connected with defence counterparts from Australia and the United Kingdom for an Aukus dialogue, and conferred with Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, chair of the Nato Military Committee.
US Pacific Command noted that Paparo carried out bilateral discussions focused on "strengthening operational cooperation, information-sharing, maritime security and readiness across the Indo-Pacific" with senior representatives from numerous partner nations.
The participating countries included Bangladesh, Brunei, Cambodia, Canada, France, India, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, Mongolia, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.
What Washington has put on record
Paparo's visit comes after a run of statements in Washington. An update on how the 2026 National Defense Strategy is being carried out, sent to the Senate Armed Services Committee, places India under the heading of burden-sharing, the idea that allies and partners should take on more of the load.
"Finally, and crucially given its regional standing and power, we are also building on our strong defence relationship with India, with the recent signature of a 10-year bilateral defence framework and a separate framework to strengthen undersea cooperation," the update said.
Testifying before lawmakers in April, Paparo said the relationship with India had seen "transformative growth through increasingly complex military exercises, defence sales, and strategic dialogue".
However, the recent Trump tariffs and the punitive measures against India for buying Russian oil, and a stuck trade deal has undoubetly strained the ties between both nations.
Paparo had also pointed to cooperation on maritime security and underwater awareness, including India's planned purchase of MQ-9B drones through US foreign military sales. He also described India as one of the partners he visits and coordinates with most often.
He said India "continues to be a source of stability within South Asia", and cited its investments in Sri Lanka and its agreements with Mauritius, which he said help keep strategic infrastructure "free of adversarial influences". On Pakistan, he noted that recent military exchanges had extended beyond traditionally disputed areas, but said India's main focus remained "maintaining deterrence and credible warfighting capability within the region writ large."
The China question in the background
None of this is discussed in isolation from China as Paparo himself has said Beijing's actions, along with its deepening ties to Russia and North Korea, make for a complex challenge to regional stability. He calls alliances and partnerships Washington's "greatest asymmetric advantage", and the Quad, which brings together the US, India, Japan and Australia, is part of that picture. Though Quad his been pushed to a back burner under the Tump 2.0.

At a regional security conference in Malaysia, Paparo said some actors were using "false claims of legitimacy" to justify coercion. "That's not the rule of law. That's the rule by law. That distinction between law as a tool of order versus law as a weapon of raw power, is the defining fault line of our time," he said. He added that the US was deterring China "through strength, not through confrontation".
In the South China Sea, Manila has accused Beijing of dangerous manoeuvres, water cannon attacks and attempts to block resupply missions around a disputed shoal. China denies this. Philippine defence secretary Gilberto Teodoro said, "China is everywhere … this is a matter of concern," and pointed to a recent Chinese ballistic missile launch into the Pacific.

articles.title: RBI may hike repo rate by 25 bps in October meet: Economists - Fortune India
articles.summary: RBI may hike repo rate by 25 bps in October meet: Economists  Fortune India
articles.full_text:
Rising inflationary pressures, resilient growth in weak global macro conditions could guide rate action
The broadening of domestic inflationary pressures and the resilience in growth despite weakening external macro-economic conditions—including foreign fund outflows—is leading economists to point out that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will start hiking interest rates sooner than expected in the October monetary policy meeting.
Economists are also forecasting an additional rate hike in December this year.
The RBI Monetary Policy Committee will meet from October 5 to 7 and is now expected to announce a 25-basis-point hike on October 7, while maintaining a neutral stance. A neutral stance will give the central bank flexibility to keep adjusting policy rates as the economic situation evolves.
The US Fed rate action in September led 30-year bond yields to rise to a multi-decade high. Yields are likely to remain high due to energy-led inflation and no clarity on whether the West Asia war will end soon.
“Our forecasts indicate possibility of Q2 inflation surpassing RBI’s forecast of 4.7% and trending closer to the upper bound of 6% as manufacturers pass on higher input costs to consumers. Further, steady growth could provide comfort to the RBI to start its hiking cycle,” says Indranil Pan, chief economist at YES Bank.
“The minutes of the August MPC meeting indicated nervousness on the inflation dynamics and called for cautious monitoring of the inflation trajectory for signs of emergence of second-round impact,” Pan said.
However, no action was taken in August as MPC members did not see the economy overheating and saw no signs of broadening inflation pressures. Given that there are signs of generalisation of price pressures, we expect the RBI to start its hiking cycle in October by 25 bps.
Pan also said that while India’s monetary policy does not strictly follow the US Fed’s, “the need to hike now may have emerged from a closing interest gap between India and US (around 165 bps now for the 2-year tenor), that is also creating the pressure for foreign flows to move out,” he said.
In September, the net FPI outflows were at $5.9 billion, of which $2.16 billion was on account of debt.
CareEdge Group’s chief economist, Rajani Sinha, and senior economist Sarbartho Mukherjee said, “The inflation outlook remains vulnerable to both external and weather risks. We project average CPI inflation of around 5.0% in FY27,” they said in a note to clients.
They also said the RBI would focus on liquidity management, as a rate hike without corresponding liquidity tightening would be ineffective.
Banks in India were able to garner a record $132.98 billion through the swap window scheme of FCNR(B) deposits by September.
Economists said the FCNR(B) inflows have also injected substantial rupee liquidity into the banking system. Daily surplus liquidity increased from an average of ₹3.7 lakh crore in August to a peak of ₹11 lakh crore in the first week of September.
With all the measures that the RBI has taken in recent weeks, systemic liquidity declined to around ₹4.8 lakh crore as of September 28, 2026, following OMO sales and VRRR auctions by the RBI. However, it is well above the average of ₹1.9 lakh crore seen during H1 CY 2026.
“The market would look for further guidance on additional measures, particularly CRR or I-CRR hikes,” the CareEdge economists said.
“We expect this policy rate hiking cycle to be shallow, with a cumulative 50–75 bps hike in the repo rate,” they added.
Most economists Fortune India spoke to indicated that the RBI Governor’s commentary and statement could be cautious.
Soumya Kanti Ghosh, Member, 16th Finance Commission & Group Chief Economic Advisor at SBI, said, “Amidst an impending global turmoil that may rip aside emerging markets with US yields at 25-year high and destined for even higher levels, the RBI is set to begin the first of the rate hikes by 25 bps.”
“We believe the balance of risks has tilted decisively towards a 25-bps rate hike at this juncture.... a combination of broadening inflationary pressures, worsening global macros, evolving liquidity conditions and a renewed global repricing of risks is making the case for pre-emptive action stronger,” he said in a note.
Goldman Sachs has also brought forward its call for the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to start its rate-hike cycle in October, from December earlier.
In a note published October 1, 2026, the brokerage expects a 25-basis-point hike each in October and December, followed by another 50 bps of tightening in the first half of 2027, taking the cumulative rate hikes in the current cycle to 100 bps.
Goldman Sachs cited stronger-than-expected growth, broadening inflation pressures and tighter global monetary conditions as reasons for the earlier start to the hiking cycle.
The report, however, said that the monsoon story deserves attention. The 2026 monsoon was the fourth driest since 2000, at just 87% of LPA, with 43% of districts receiving deficient rainfall.
Punjab and Bihar received 41% and 32% below-normal rainfall, respectively, while Maharashtra has declared drought across 265 talukas. “With low irrigation coverage for crops such as soybean, tur, jowar and bajra, rainfall dependence remains high, while strong El Niño conditions and below-normal October rainfall could pose further risks to Rabi output.”
Ghosh said that they expect RBI to upgrade the GDP forecasts upwards by 30 bps and inflation forecast by 20 bps for FY27.
In a September report, Crisil had said that rainfall deficiency has widened to 14% so far this season, worse than expected for the southwest monsoon. “Although sowing has progressed well, it does not mean the crop sector is out of danger. The focus of concern has shifted from acreage to yields, and crop incomes are likely to moderate as a result,” its chief economist Dharmakirti Joshi and Deshpande said.
The data shows that monsoon shocks do sting crops, but, as seen in previous decades, they have not necessarily translated into higher food inflation.

articles.title: Munich Oktoberfest ride gives women free shorts amid thousands of upskirting videos - The Times of India
articles.summary: Munich Oktoberfest ride gives women free shorts amid thousands of upskirting videos  The Times of IndiaSee more headlines and perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
A popular ride at Munich's Oktoberfest has become the centre of a growing controversy over voyeuristic videos, with its operator handing out free cycling shorts to women to help protect them from being filmed under their skirts.
The Teufelsrad, or Devil's Wheel, is one of the oldest attractions at the annual beer festival. Its large circular platform spins at increasing speeds, eventually throwing riders off. The movement can cause skirts and dresses to fly up, making people on the ride vulnerable to being filmed from below.
Thousands of videos showing women on the attraction have appeared online, with some reportedly attracting millions of views. German broadcaster BR reported that one woman earned €9,000 from a single clip.
Thousands of videos circulating online
At least 32,000 videos featuring women on the Teufelsrad have been circulated, according to Munich daily Süddeutsche Zeitung. Some have apparently been watched millions of times.
The videos often show women wearing traditional dirndl dresses with their underwear visible. Some images have also been digitally manipulated to make the women appear naked, according to BR.
BR's investigation found that a group of professional YouTubers from Ukraine and several people from Bavaria were behind the videos.
Filming under someone's skirt is illegal in Germany and can carry a prison sentence of up to two years. However, critics say the law does not cover every situation in which intimate images are captured.
Josephine Ballon, head of German non-profit organisation Hate Aid, which supports victims of digital violence, said the existing law does not offer enough protection. She said there are plans for new legislation, but the current law "applies only when you film under the skirt", meaning it may not apply when a skirt simply flies up and someone photographs what is visible.
Ballon also warned that new devices such as camera glasses could create additional risks.
Ride operator gives women free cycling shorts
Elisabeth Polaczy, who runs the Teufelsrad, told the BBC that she has been giving women and girls wearing dresses free cycling shorts for the past three years.
She said she has handed out more than 100 pairs during this year's Oktoberfest.
"I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure."
Polaczy, who is 80, said providing the shorts costs her money but gives her peace of mind.
The Teufelsrad tent displays signs and police posters in both German and English warning visitors against filming under people's skirts. However, Polaczy said it is impossible to monitor everyone using a smartphone in the crowded area.
Some waitresses working at this year's festival have also started wearing cycling shorts beneath their dirndls.
Police step up warnings as influencers face new rules
Bavarian police have been running a poster campaign at Oktoberfest since 2025 to warn visitors about upskirting, a spokesman told the BBC.
Police arrested a 45-year-old Swiss man this year after he was allegedly caught using his phone to film under a German woman's dirndl. There were 10 arrests for upskirting at the festival last year and seven in 2024.
Ballon said people who upload intimate images online should face consequences, as should platforms that host such material.
The issue comes as Munich authorities are also tightening rules for influencers and content creators who make money from filming at Oktoberfest.
The city has banned live streaming from the festival and requires people who want to film there to obtain a permit for a fee. Hundreds of permits have been issued this year to influencers who earn money through activities such as product placements and sponsorships.

Later, Ram Mohan Naidu highlighted that the Mulapeta-Pundi region already has strong infrastructure, including port, national highway and railway connectivity, besides future air connectivity, making it highly suitable for heavy industries.

For the proposed smelter, the possibility of sourcing alumina from Angul in Odisha is being explored. This would create a link between Odisha’s alumina industry and Andhra Pradesh’s coastal industrial and port infrastructure, he added.
Ram Mohan Naidu said Union Minister Kishan Reddy responded positively to the proposal and that a central inspection team from the Ministry of Mines is scheduled to visit the designated locations within a week to assess land feasibility and infrastructure requirements.
He mentioned that further steps would be coordinated with the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) and the Andhra Pradesh government regarding the use of saline land and industrial development.
Additionally, Ram Mohan Naidu highlighted that the proposal could significantly boost industrialisation and infrastructure in Uttarandhra.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia readies 100,000 Yemeni troops for Houthi assault: Can fragmented Yemeni forces retake Bab el - The Times of India
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia readies 100,000 Yemeni troops for Houthi assault: Can fragmented Yemeni forces retake Bab el  The Times of IndiaSaudis plan assault on Houthis to break Red Sea chokehold  ReutersWhy Trump May Want to Avoid Messing With the Houthis  PoliticoSaudis plan major offensive against the Houthis, but U.S. won't join for now  AxiosIran Update, October 2, 2026  Critical Threats
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia is preparing an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen, with Riyadh weighing a limited coastal assault around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait or a broader multi-front operation.
According to Reuters, the offensive could be launched in the coming weeks and would be led by Yemeni forces and backed by Saudi air strikes.
The report, citing six people familiar with the preparations, said more than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilised depending on the scale of the operation, while the timing remains uncertain, with estimates ranging from within a week to after the US midterm elections in early November.
The immediate objective of the planned offensive is to reverse the Houthis' rapid gains last month, when the group advanced down Yemen's Red Sea coast and seized control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to people familiar with the Saudi preparations cited by Reuters.
Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit of the Red Sea and a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia. The route has gained greater importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict.
Michael Ratney, a former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, said he expected the operation to be more limited than the Saudi-led intervention in Yemen that began in 2015.
“Ideally, it would be a fairly limited operation to retake coastal areas and get back to normal maritime traffic,” Ratney said, according to Reuters.
Ratney's assessment points to the immediate military objective being focused on the Red Sea coast rather than an attempt to defeat the Houthis across Yemen.
Saudi Arabia's problem on the ground
The biggest challenge for Riyadh is the condition of the Yemeni forces that would lead the ground offensive. The force is a collection of factions armed and trained by Saudi Arabia and the UAE rather than a unified military, and those groups have competing political and territorial interests.
Yemen analyst Mohammed Albasha told Reuters that many anti-Houthi forces are still “not organised or prepared” for the sustained offensive needed to push back the Houthis, who are applying pressure across several fronts.
The anti-Houthi camp was further fractured last winter when UAE-backed southern fighters clashed with Saudi-backed forces after trying to seize territory in eastern Yemen.
Ali Shihabi, a Saudi political analyst close to government thinking, also said the outcome would depend on the performance of the local forces, with the ground campaign moving from defending positions to going on the offensive.
Where are Saudi Arabia's allies?
Saudi Arabia's allies are backing Riyadh mainly through intelligence, equipment and defensive support rather than direct combat in Yemen.
The United States, Saudi Arabia's most powerful ally, is providing military advisers and intelligence, including targeting information for Saudi air operations.
However, Reuters reported that President Donald Trump had previously rejected Saudi requests for direct US military support, including air strikes, leaving Riyadh to conduct the air campaign itself.
A separate pillar of Saudi security is the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey on August 7.
The pact says an armed attack on one of the three countries will be treated as an attack on all. But Pakistan has so far stopped short of committing combat forces to Yemen.
Islamabad has instead sent air-defence systems, light artillery, drones and anti-drone equipment, while 30,000 to 40,000 Pakistani troops are deployed inside Saudi Arabia for border defence and missile and drone interception.
Turkey has also supplied military equipment and Turkish drones are being used over Yemen, while France has announced defensive systems and troops for the protection of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Yanbu.
The military chiefs of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey met in Riyadh on September 25 to discuss the situation, while Pakistan's foreign minister said on October 2 that the three countries would hold an emergency meeting in Riyadh next week.

articles.title: Why RBI may hike policy rates next week? - bfsi.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.summary: Why RBI may hike policy rates next week?  bfsi.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.full_text:
The case for advancing the first rate hike to October has strengthened as inflation is set to breach 5% in September and potentially peak in October-December, while global crude oil prices have remained above USD100 a barrel.
| CPI inflation is expected to breach 5% in September and could peak in October-December, while crude oil prices above USD100 a barrel add to upside risks. April-June GDP growth at 7.8% was 80 basis points above the RBI's forecast, while high-frequency indicators for July-August continue to point to resilient growth. The RBI is expected to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% on October 7, retain a neutral stance and raise rates by another 25 basis points in December to 5.75%. Despite surplus system liquidity, financial conditions have tightened, with benchmark bond yields above 7% and continued FPI outflows, while the RBI is expected to continue absorbing excess liquidity. |  | 
The case for advancing the first rate hike to October has strengthened as inflation is set to breach 5% in September and potentially peak in October-December, while global crude oil prices have remained above USD100 a barrel. Stronger-than-expected April-June GDP growth and resilient high-frequency indicators for July-August could also prompt the RBI to revise up both its inflation and growth forecasts. The assessment is from Barclays.
August CPI inflation rose to 4.8% year-on-year from 4.45% in July, driven by higher food and fuel inflation. While inflation generalisation remains limited, 38 of 198 items in the core CPI basket recorded inflation of 4% or more in August, up from 36 in July. The report said the MPC may respond pre-emptively as higher inflation broadens further.
The RBI may also revise its FY27 CPI inflation forecast from the current 5%, with Barclays forecasting 4.8% and highlighting upside risks. In the August MPC meeting, one member said it would be reasonable to assume oil prices close to USD90 a barrel. With crude now elevated above USD100, the report sees a possibility of further pass-through to retail prices.
If global oil prices remain above USD100 a barrel, Barclays expects another round of retail fuel price increases, possibly after Diwali, creating further risks to retail inflation. WPI and PPI inflation in August were also trending above 9% year-on-year.
Growth strong
Growth has meanwhile remained stronger than the RBI had expected. GDP growth in the April-June quarter was 7.8% year-on-year, 80 basis points above the RBI's 7% forecast. While high-frequency indicators for July-August showed some moderation, the report said the narrative of robust growth continues. Barclays expects the RBI to revise its FY27 real GDP growth forecast up from 6.7%, with its own growth forecast at 7.1%.
The report expects the October hike to be accompanied by a “neutral” stance, with the RBI retaining optionality rather than indicating a series of rate increases. A second and final 25 basis point hike is expected in December, taking the terminal repo rate to 5.75%, alongside a possible shift in stance to “calibrated tightening”.
Financial conditions have also tightened since the August MPC meeting. Barclays' financial conditions indicator rose to 0.90 on September 28 from 0.66 on August 5, with most of the tightening coming through the government securities and equity markets.
Benchmark government bond yields have risen above 7%, alongside higher US Treasury yields and energy prices above USD105 a barrel. Continued FPI outflows and the unresolved Middle East conflict have also weighed on financial conditions.
At the same time, liquidity conditions remain relatively easy. System liquidity was around 1.8% of NDTL in surplus and the weighted average call rate was 5.1% as of September 28, below the repo rate. Barclays expects the RBI to continue liquidity absorption through overnight and term VRRR operations, OMO sales and swaps.
FCNR, ECB and OFCB inflows of USD143.6 billion between June 8 and August 31 had added substantially to domestic rupee liquidity. The report expects liquidity tightening to continue alongside monetary tightening to ensure effective transmission, while higher currency demand during the festive season and continued intervention in the spot foreign exchange market could also drain liquidity.
The expected October move is therefore being viewed as a “monetary policy calibration” in response to the normalisation of inflation, with Barclays expecting the RBI to keep its neutral stance initially and retain flexibility on the pace of further tightening.

articles.title: Distance between learning today and living tomorrow - The New Indian Express
articles.summary: Distance between learning today and living tomorrow  The New Indian Express
articles.full_text:
The NEET exam question paper leak, and youth protests across India since June, speak volumes about the state of India’s education system. The New Education Policy (NEP), 2020 is itself caught in controversy—with four-year courses teaching students all kinds of superfluous material they hate, as it has actually reduced substantive course content. Students learn less in four years than in the erstwhile three-year undergraduate programme—not to mention mass faculty appointments driven by ideological inclinations. These crises, wrought upon the students, have fed on a rapidly privatising higher education system. The emergence of an unprecedented movement by the Cockroach Janta Party is the outcome.
However, these problems are merely the tip of a systemic crisis in education. India wants to compete with China in deep tech and become ‘viksit’. But far from being able to compete, India’s higher education system has only recently moved to massify enrolment, going from 11 percent gross enrolment ratio (GER) in 2006 to 27 percent by 2017, and 29 percent in 2024—only to achieve extremely low employability and rising graduate unemployment. The irony is that the NEP 2020 still targets 50 percent GER in higher education by 2035.
This massification so far was built upon very shaky foundations: literacy was barely 51 percent when India launched its economic reform programme in 1991, due to a 40-year neglect of school and vocational education—reflecting the blasé approach of policymaking elites to rising child labour. In response, finally, public expenditures on schools rose in the later nineties. First, elementary schooling was universalised by 2010 then secondary by 2015, with gender parity. Rapid school massification ensured learning levels were going to remain poor—as demonstrated for two decades by the annual state of education reports.
These rapid massifications of schools in the nineties and noughties and then of higher education enrolment have had three educational and, hence, labour market outcomes. First, the education/skill composition of India’s workforce remains appalling. Illiteracy remains frighteningly high at over one-fifth of the total population (over one-fourth for women) in 2024. Workers with eight years or below of schooling account for another 19 and 21 percent, respectively. Thus, nearly two-thirds of India’s current workforce barely has eight or fewer years of schooling. Also, merely 2.4 percent of the workforce has formal vocational training (VET) and another 4.7 percent any higher education technical training in 2024—though the NEP 2020 aspires to take VET enrolment to a colossal 50 percent.
Second, with such a poorly educated workforce, it is not surprising that 90 percent of India’s workforce toils in the informal sector, lacking the skills to secure a formal job in larger enterprises. This statistic has not changed for the last two recorded decades.
Third, as the quality of learning is poor at both school and higher education levels, open unemployment among youths has grown. It used to be only six percent among aged 15-29 years in 2011-12, but tripled to 18 percent by 2017-18.
Jobs growth collapsed in smaller businesses the year after the globally-unprecedented, “revolutionary” decision to demonetise 86 percent of India’s currency. Then a poorly-designed and ill-implemented GST regime caused further massive closure and downturn. This was followed by growth slowing each quarter till Covid. Finally, as job growth collapsed and 8 crore workers spiralled down to agriculture and related activities between 2020 and 2024, people finally began to ask: can India really take advantage of its demographic dividend?
A rising share of the working-age population, if they get quality formal-sector non-farm jobs, would actually contribute to the growth of India’s economy. When the share of such workforce rises while that of dependents falls, then the country truly realises its demographic dividend.
India has managed to grow slowly—and much less inclusively—partly because its workforce is poorly educated. As we show in our latest book India Out of Work: Rethinking India's Growth Story, only 2.4 percent of the 61-crore strong Indian workforce is formally trained in any vocation. A far more skilled and better educated Vietnam and China attracted more foreign investment into manufacturing. Meanwhile, with a shallow vocational education system, India’s youth with higher-secondary certificates stream into tertiary education of indifferent employability.
Digging deeper for reasons of poor employability, we find that massification of undergraduate education occurred through growth of private colleges. Affiliated colleges grew at a rate of 4 new colleges per day for 20 years. Without a weekend’s break! And most are private. Total affiliated college numbers grew from over 10,000 at the turn of the century to nearly 58,000 within 25 years.
The private share of rising higher education enrolment rose as governments did not increase public spending commensurate to rising demand. Trouble is, central or state universities have little ability to monitor these private colleges—hence both quality and employability collapse.
If we wish to prepare workers ready for the transition into the world of work, they need not continue into higher education. Surplus enrolment needs a diversion to VET—provided it takes place with employer and industry engagement. In-enterprise training, in the form of apprenticeships, after taking industry-designed VET courses, would ensure a seamless transition to work. But that means training should become demand-based, employer-driven and government-managed.
Another reason for employability issues is the composition of subjects higher education students studied. By way of contrast, Vietnam currently produces roughly 50-70 percent more tertiary science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) students per young person in the population than India does, because it combines higher overall participation in higher education and a larger STEM share within it.
One can see a similar trend in Tamil Nadu, one of India’s most industrialised states. Not only does the state have a higher education enrolment ratio of 48 (more than Vietnam’s), but nearly 30 percent of its higher education students are in STEM subjects. The policy implications are clear.
Santosh Mehrotra | Professor of economics, Jawaharlal Nehru University

articles.title: India Pushes Chile Pact, Opens Mexico Talks - StratNews Global
articles.summary: India Pushes Chile Pact, Opens Mexico Talks  StratNews Global
articles.full_text:
India is stepping up trade engagement with Latin America, with negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) with Chile targeted for completion by the end of 2026 and formal trade negotiations with Mexico expected to begin later this month.
The two initiatives form part of India’s efforts to expand its network of trade agreements as tariffs, regulatory requirements and other market-access conditions become more important factors in international trade.
The India-Chile CEPA is one of the key elements of the effort. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal met Chile’s Vice-Minister for International Economic Relations Paula Estévez Weinstein in Santiago on August 26 to review progress in the negotiations. India reiterated its commitment to concluding the agreement this year.
The proposed CEPA would go beyond the existing preferential trade agreement (PTA) between the two countries and establish a broader framework covering trade, investment and economic cooperation. The areas identified for greater cooperation include healthcare and pharmaceuticals, energy, minerals, agriculture, machinery and engineering, as well as technology, talent and supply-chain resilience.
“Bilateral trade between Chile and India exceeded USD 5.6 billion in 2025, reflecting the growing importance of the partnership,” Chile’s Ambassador to India, Juan Angulo M, told StratNewsGlobal.
According to Angulo, the CEPA is intended to deepen trade, investment and economic cooperation between the two countries.
India and Chile already have a preferential trade agreement, which was expanded in 2017. The proposed CEPA would take the existing trading relationship into a broader framework.
For India, the negotiations cover market access for exporters as well as investment and cooperation in areas including critical minerals and energy. Chile, meanwhile, is an important source of minerals and a market for Indian goods and services.
The next milestone in India’s Latin America trade engagement could come later this month, when India and Mexico are expected to sign the Terms of Reference (ToR) for formal trade negotiations.
The ToR would not constitute a trade agreement. Instead, it would establish the framework and scope of the negotiations and provide the basis for discussions on market access and other areas of economic cooperation. India has been working with Mexico to finalise the framework. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal is expected to travel to Mexico to take the process forward and formally launch the negotiations.
Mexico is an important market for Indian exporters, particularly in automobiles and auto components, pharmaceuticals, engineering products and chemicals. The terms eventually negotiated by the two sides will determine the extent of any improvement in market access and the benefits for exporters.
Mexico’s position in North American supply chains is also relevant to Indian companies seeking to diversify their manufacturing and export networks.
The Chile and Mexico initiatives are taking place alongside India’s negotiations with other Latin American economies.
External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, speaking at the India-CELAC Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in New York, said India was seeking “robust and balanced economic partnerships” in the region through the proposed CEPA with Chile, an FTA with Peru and an expansion of the preferential trade arrangement with MERCOSUR.
The negotiations are part of India’s broader effort to expand preferential market access for its exporters. Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has said India’s trade agreements could eventually provide preferential access to economies accounting for around 75 per cent of global GDP.
For Indian exporters, trade agreements are also becoming more relevant as market access is shaped not only by tariffs but by climate-related regulations, technical standards and other non-tariff barriers.
With Chile and Mexico, India is pursuing two separate trade tracks in Latin America: one aimed at upgrading an existing preferential arrangement into a wider economic partnership, and another at establishing a formal framework for negotiations with one of the region’s largest economies.

articles.title: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon once again 'warns' Europe 'you may be losing', offers 'big, beautiful solu - The Times of India
articles.summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon once again 'warns' Europe 'you may be losing', offers 'big, beautiful solu  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Jamie Dimon, the CEO of America’s largest bank JPMorgan Chase has renewed his warning that Europe risks falling behind economically, while proposing what he called a ‘big beautiful’ free-trade agreement with the United States as part of a broader effort to strengthen the Western alliance. In an opinion piece published in The Wall Street Journal, Dimon argued that Washington should offer Europe a sweeping economic partnership if the continent implements meaningful economic and military reforms designed to boost growth, competitiveness and security. “I believe the U.S. should offer Europe a major inducement: If it executes meaningful economic and military reforms... the US will negotiate one big, beautiful economic and free-trade agreement with Europe,” Dimon wrote.
Jamie Dimon calls for deeper economic integration 
According to Dimon, such an agreement would go beyond Europe and could eventually be extended to friendly democracies including Canada, Mexico, Japan, South Korea, Australia and the Philippines.
He described deeper economic integration among democratic allies as a potential “game changer” that would allow them to set global trade rules, strengthen economic resilience and present a united front against geopolitical pressures.
Dimon's proposal contrasts with the more protectionist approach adopted by the administration of Donald Trump, whose tariff policies have strained relations with several trading partners, including the European Union and Canada.
What Europe needs to fix, according to Jamie Dimon
Dimon's op-ed didn't just float a vague aspiration — it named specific reforms he believes are prerequisites. He called on the European Union to finally complete its long-delayed Capital Markets Union and Banking Union to boost competitiveness, to follow through on the recommendations laid out in the Draghi report, and to secure genuine independence in defense, manufacturing, and energy.
He argued that a Europe capable of mobilizing capital, scaling innovative companies, consolidating defense production, and reducing strategic dependencies would emerge as a stronger security partner, a more resilient economic partner, and a more credible counterweight to China's growing economic influence.
Vision for a stronger Western alliance
Beyond Europe, Dimon argued that the United States must also take steps to preserve its position as the world's leading economic and military power. He called for renewed focus on strengthening the American economy, expanding opportunity and reinforcing democratic alliances.
According to Dimon, a combination of US leadership and successful European reforms could create a stronger Western bloc capable of driving economic growth and addressing long-term geopolitical challenges.
“A renewed commitment to American values and alliances coupled with bold reforms by Europe would be a geopolitical and economic home run, guaranteeing the Western world's strength for the next 250 years,” he wrote.
Not the first time JPMorgan CEO delivered this message
This isn't the first time Dimon has bluntly criticized Europe's economic standing. Last year, speaking to European business and political leaders at an event in Ireland, he delivered an even more direct version of the same warning, telling the room flatly that, compared with the US and Asia, Europe is losing.

articles.summary: SBI Research sees CPI inflation at 5.65% in Sept, above 6.5% in Oct-Nov  bfsi.economictimes.indiatimes.com
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: SBI Research expects CPI inflation to rise to around 5.65 per cent in September and cross 6.5 per cent in October and November, before easing below 6 per cent in early 2027.
In its pre-Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) report released on Friday, SBI Research said the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) may raise the policy repo rate by at least 25 basis points at its October 5-7 monetary policy meeting, citing rising inflation, global risks and pressure on the rupee.
Also Read: Need reforms for higher recoveries and speedier resolutions in IBC: IBBI Chair
"We believe the balance of risks has tilted decisively towards a 25-bps rate hike at this juncture," the report said.
Also Read: Foreign capital is slipping away. Can India lure investors back?
At its August 3-5 meeting, the MPC unanimously kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25 per cent and retained its neutral stance. The RBI had said it wanted greater clarity on the direction and composition of inflation before taking further policy action.
According to SBI Research, inflationary pressures have strengthened since the August policy meeting. Retail inflation rose to 4.82 per cent in August from 4.45 per cent in July, with price pressures spreading across a wider range of items.
The report said 22 commodities accounted for 90 per cent of the weighted contribution to CPI inflation in January. By August, the number had increased to 51, indicating that inflationary pressures had become more broad-based.
SBI Research also highlighted weakness in the rupee as a key risk. It attributed the pressure on the currency to a strong US dollar, foreign currency demand from oil marketing companies and corporates, and continued selling by foreign portfolio investors.
The research house also flagged risks from the weak monsoon. The 2026 southwest monsoon stood at 87 per cent of the long-period average, while 43 per cent of districts received deficient rainfall.SBI Research said strong El Nino conditions and below-normal rainfall in October could pose risks to Rabi crops and add to food inflation pressures.
The research house expects the RBI to raise its FY27 GDP growth forecast by 30 basis points and its inflation projection by 20 basis points at the October policy review.
The RBI's October MPC meeting is scheduled to be held from October 5 to 7.

articles.title: A WORLD IN REBALANCING - The Indian Panorama
articles.summary: A WORLD IN REBALANCING  The Indian Panorama
articles.full_text:
Everybody is openly dealing with everybody else. That is where we are heading toward multipolarity.
- I.S. Saluja
NEW YORK (TIP): India’s External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar offered a wide-ranging assessment of a world undergoing profound geopolitical and economic change during a conversation with former U.S. diplomat Daniel Russel at the Asia Society in New York on September 28, 2026.
Speaking at the conclusion of a busy United Nations General Assembly High-Level Week, during which he said he had met 85 ministers from different countries over ten days, Jaishankar described an international system increasingly shaped by competition, interdependence, strategic autonomy and the emergence of multiple centers of power.
The old playbook, he suggested, is being rewritten.
Countries that once expected others to align themselves more rigidly with particular blocs are themselves pursuing multiple relationships. Trade arrangements are changing. Conflicts in Ukraine and the Gulf are producing consequences far beyond the countries directly involved. Developing nations are confronting pressures involving energy, food, fertilizer and finance. And governments are increasingly seeking multiple partnerships rather than placing their interests entirely in one relationship.
For India, Jaishankar argued, the answer lies neither in isolation nor rigid alignment, but in maintaining stable and reliable relationships across a broad spectrum of powers while preserving strategic autonomy.
In an engaging conversation, Russel challenged the Minister on whether such multipolarity could deteriorate into a “Hobbesian” world dominated by raw national self-interest. Jaishankar acknowledged the risks but argued that countries’ own need for stability and predictability would ultimately encourage balancing arrangements and new partnerships.
The discussion also turned candidly to India-U.S. relations. Jaishankar identified trade, terrorism and mobility among issues affecting the relationship, while expressing hope that bilateral ties would return to an upward trajectory. On China, he said relations had improved as the border situation moved toward greater normalcy, although he stopped short of describing the change as structural. With Japan, he saw considerable potential in investment, technology, defense, supply-chain diversification and greater societal exchanges.
Edited excerpts from the conversation follow:
Bharat Khera
DANIEL RUSSEL: Minister, welcome back to Asia Society. In your opening remarks you spoke about the competitive spirit colliding with the realities of interdependence and weaponization.
When we spoke on this stage two years ago, I asked you about the paradox of India dealing simultaneously with Washington, Beijing, Moscow and others. You explained that one could “walk and chew gum at the same time.”
Looking at the world you have described today, I would like a piece of that gum.
Let me begin with the United States. You have spoken previously about consequential changes in the international system and an erosion of established rules. What changes do you see, what has been their impact, and who have been the winners and losers?
S. JAISHANKAR: That piece of gum is now in pretty big supply in Washington.
This was a question people normally asked us: How are you dealing with China, Russia, Ukraine, other parts of Asia and Europe simultaneously?
Today Washington itself is practicing that approach with a great deal of gusto.
There was a time when the narrative was: “We don’t like you having too many options. We want you to focus your relationship on us”—even though the United States, being a global power, kept more of its own options open.
Today that pretense has dropped for everybody.
Everybody is openly dealing with everybody else. That is where we are heading toward multipolarity.
Everybody is going to try to get the best deal possible from a given situation based upon a sharper definition of national interest. We may like it or not, but once Washington takes the lead in that direction, it becomes something of a global fashion.
On rules, however, I think there may be some confusion. I did not say that the United States was primarily responsible for departing from the rules.
My point has been that rules—particularly economic rules—have been continuously eroded over time.
We have trading structures based on market assumptions, while trading practices have departed sharply from those assumptions. A great many non-market practices entered the trading system, and for whatever reasons the world looked away.
So the observance of rules was gradually corroded rather than simply rejected.
Now we are seeing new positions from the world’s largest economy and a different trading template based increasingly on one-to-one deals. That strikes at some of the assumptions underlying the earlier system.
We are therefore seeing greater realism, a different template and a renegotiation of many arrangements.
What emerges will be a new set of bargains, understandings and possibly relationships. Countries will agree on some issues and cooperate to different degrees on others.
We have to throw away the old playbook and start writing a new one.
That will not happen overnight.
RUSSEL: The postwar international system rested, at least in principle, on the strongest country accepting that rules were binding on it as well. That provided predictability and safeguards, particularly for smaller countries.
If the major powers are no longer prepared to accept broadly common rules, what prevents multipolarity from becoming a Hobbesian jungle—a survival-of-the-fittest, dog-eat-dog environment?
JAISHANKAR: From the perspective of a country such as India, there is another problem.
Complaints about the trading system may arise from the behavior of one country, but the reactions are then visited upon us as well. That is rather unfair.
There is one conversation about how the trading system was gamed, how trading practices evolved, how surpluses were created, market shares increased and production shifted.
But what has now happened is something closer to the United States versus everybody else—including countries that had no role in gaming that system.
Whether we like it or not, that is American policy today.
How do we prevent this from becoming utterly Hobbesian? We will have to see whether checks and safety nets emerge that limit the competition, or whether the United States deals individually with 190-odd countries and the aggregate of those bilateral arrangements itself becomes the system.
We could end up much more in the direction you describe.
If you are negotiating in today’s world, you need that sense of realism.
RUSSEL: Then what would a healthier version of multipolarity look like—one that respects, for example, the interests of developing countries? How can the self-interest of major powers be tempered into something more stable and equitable?
JAISHANKAR: That is really at the heart of the foreign-policy thinking of countries of our size and range of interests.
First, you build a reputation for being stable, consistent and reliable, so that in a dynamic and volatile world others see you as a steadying factor. Partners then tend to gravitate toward you.
Second, the more you diversify relationships and identify common interests and common ground, the greater the possibility of creating a balancing structure.
We need to temper self-interest with long-term predictability and stability—which are themselves part of intelligent self-interest.
Take India. We would ask: how do we achieve the right balance in our relationships with the United States, Europe, Japan, China, Russia, the Gulf, ASEAN and the Global South?
It is almost a portfolio-management approach.
The Hobbesian scenario you describe is extremely volatile and risky. Countries will not want to expose their trade and economies indefinitely to that degree of volatility.
They will seek relationships offering stability and predictability, even where the immediate returns may be lower.
I am therefore not pessimistic.
The world is becoming more competitive. It is tough. A new dynamic and a new culture will emerge. New negotiations will take place and new bargains will be struck.
When the smoke clears, the different points will be joined by lines of different lengths, and a new geometry will emerge.
RUSSEL: There are at least two forces complicating that vision. One is the ripple effect from conflicts—whether Ukraine or the Gulf—which creates enormous consequences for energy, grain and other necessities in countries far removed from those wars.
The second is the increasing extraterritorial application of sanctions and rules by major powers, which can force third countries to choose sides.
How does India view those pressures?
JAISHANKAR: They are a major concern for us.
The Ukraine conflict and now the Iran-Gulf conflict have had a devastating impact on Global South economies.
Energy markets are already extremely tight. If politics is added to the security-of-supply problem, prices rise precisely when countries should be trying to stabilize them.
Food is another concern. Major grain exporters may be unable to send shipments, particularly through the Black Sea. We are also looking at significant fertilizer shortages because important producers are located in Russia and the Middle East and production has been affected.
If you combine an energy crunch with pressures involving food, fertilizer and finance—because money moves toward safe havens whenever conflict erupts—the result is extraordinarily stressful for developing economies.
Policymakers cannot simply say these consequences were unintended.
They have a responsibility to consider the impact their decisions will have on other countries.
Countries cannot be so self-centered that they make decisions entirely within their own world and then tell everyone else: “It wasn’t my intention to make your life difficult.”
We also cannot allow countries to be left behind
